Starting January 1, your health insurer has to hand your medical history to your doctor automatically — unless you opt out. It has to hand that same history to your next insurer only if you opt in.
 
 Two federal requirements, one deadline, opposite defaults. One of them will carry real volume on day one and the other almost certainly will not, and most implementation plans treat them as the same project.
 
 There's a second wrinkle for hospitals.  Four months out, the useful test isn't whether the connection works. It's whether it returns the patients you're actually treating, with enough history to be worth reading.

title: LinkedIn post by Adam Gupilan
text_or_description:
The Prior Authorization API under CMS-0057-F takes effect January 1, 2027. A little over three months.

Almost everything written about it is about speed — requests moving through an API instead of a fax queue. From the review chair, that's not the part that matters.

The load-bearing line is in CMS's own fact sheet. The API has to be populated with the payer's list of covered items and services, and it has to identify documentation requirements for prior authorization approval.

That's the criteria checklist. Published, and queryable before the note is written.

Most denials I see aren't clinical disagreements. The care was right, and the note answered a different question than the criteria asked. That checklist has always existed. It just lived on the payer's side of the wall.

Two things to stay clear-eyed about.

The API carries the request. It does not make the decision. A submission that still doesn't establish what the criteria ask gets denied faster, not less.

And the scope is narrower than the coverage suggests. Impacted payers are Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service and managed care, and QHP issuers on the federally facilitated exchanges. Medicare fee-for-service isn't on that list. Neither are commercial group plans.

One thing already in effect that fewer offices use than should: since 2026, impacted payers have had to give a specific reason for a denied prior authorization — by portal, fax, email, mail, or phone. If your denials still say "not medically necessary" and stop there, that's a question you can ask today, not in January.

text_or_description:
A 1–2% Medicare reimbursement change may look small on paper.

For an independent medical practice, it isn't.

CMS has proposed its 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule, and the numbers deserve attention.

Under the proposal:

→ Qualifying APM conversion factor: $33.17
→ Non-qualifying APM conversion factor: $32.84

That represents a projected decline from the current 2026 conversion factors.

But here’s the bigger issue:

Practices cannot manage reimbursement only after the claim is submitted.

Revenue performance starts much earlier.

It starts with:

Patient eligibility
↓
Correct documentation
↓
Diagnosis + CPT selection
↓
Modifiers
↓
Medical necessity
↓
Prior authorization
↓
Clean claim submission
↓
Payment / denial
↓
Denial resolution

CMS is also proposing changes around E/M services, G2211, remote monitoring, behavioral health, FQHC/RHC services and value-based care.

That means the EHR and RCM system should not operate as two separate worlds.

A modern EHR should help the provider understand:

“What did I document?”

But it should also help the organization understand:

“Will we get paid correctly for the care we delivered?”

That connection between clinical workflow and financial workflow is where I believe the next generation of healthcare technology has to go.

Because improving revenue cycle isn't only about collecting faster.

It's about preventing revenue leakage before the claim ever leaves the practice.

For U.S. clinic owners and healthcare leaders:

Where do you see the biggest revenue leakage today — documentation, coding, prior authorization, denials, or collections?

The Medicare Advantage Improvement Act Just Cleared Its First Hurdle — What H.R. 8375 Would Mean for HH and Hospice Cash Flow

H.R. 8375 — the Medicare Advantage Improvement Act of 2026 — has picked up bipartisan support and endorsement from AHA, AAHomecare, and LeadingAge since its April 2026 introduction. If it moves, the friction that has strangled home health and hospice MA margins for the last five years changes materially.

Most owners are treating this as political noise. It is worth reading the text.

What the bill actually does that hits your P&L:

1. Standard prior authorization decisions in 72 hours, expedited in 24 hours. Today many MA plans stretch decisions past two weeks, delaying starts of care and inflating your DSO. Compressed decision windows would move revenue forward by 10–20 days on affected episodes.

2. Coverage criteria must align with traditional Medicare. Plans could no longer apply stricter medical necessity thresholds than fee-for-service. That kills a significant portion of the denial rationale used against home health episodes and hospice general inpatient stays.

3. No re-authorization on services already approved or when a clinician makes clinically necessary changes mid-episode. This is the single biggest source of mid-episode revenue leakage most agencies do not track separately.

4. Expanded access requirements for post-acute providers, including home medical equipment and home-based care. Narrow-network MA behavior would face new statutory constraints.

Even if the bill stalls in this Congress, three things are already happening:
— CMS is signaling alignment through its own prior authorization rulemaking
— MA plans that overreach on prior auth are visible political targets
— The 25+ health systems dropping MA contracts in 2026 have shifted the negotiating floor

What you should be doing regardless of the bill's timeline:
— Track prior auth turnaround time by MA plan as a monthly KPI
— Document mid-episode reauthorization requests separately from initial denials
— Build appeal cost per denied episode into your MA contract profitability analysis

If the reform passes, agencies with clean data will capture the cash flow benefit first. If it stalls, that same data is your negotiating leverage at contract renewal.

Good front-end revenue cycle management isn’t simply obtaining authorization.

It’s knowing exactly what is required before the patient receives care.

That protects patient access, staff time, and reimbursement.

text_or_description:
Administrative Complexity Is Becoming a Clinical Problem

Prior authorization, claim denials, and payer documentation requirements are often described as revenue cycle challenges.

Technically, that is true.

But it may also understate the broader impact they have on healthcare organizations.

When administrative requirements consume clinical time, delay treatment, and reduce organizational capacity, they are no longer simply financial problems.

They become care delivery problems.

That is one reason I found the American Hospital Association’s recent Cost of Caring report particularly important. The report notes that Medicare Advantage plans issued nearly 50 million prior authorization requests in 2023 and that hospitals spent approximately $26 billion managing insurance claims. It also found that 70% of denied claims were eventually paid, but only after additional reviews and administrative work.

That is an extraordinary amount of effort devoted to determining whether organizations will be paid for care they have already delivered.

The cost is not limited to billing departments.

Physicians participate in peer-to-peer reviews.

Nurses provide additional documentation.

Patients wait for decisions.

Administrative teams track, resubmit, appeal, and reconcile information across multiple systems.

The most effective healthcare finance leaders I have worked with understand that administrative efficiency and clinical capacity are increasingly connected.

Every unnecessary administrative task competes with something else the organization could be doing.

That might be caring for another patient, resolving a genuine clinical issue, improving the patient experience, or investing in growth.

Healthcare has spent years treating administrative complexity as an unavoidable feature of the system.

I suspect that view is becoming financially and operationally unsustainable.

Reducing administrative burden may ultimately prove to be one of the most important clinical capacity strategies available to healthcare organizations.

title: LinkedIn post by Josh Schweizer
text_or_description:
A TMS billing policy change doesn't have to introduce a new CPT code to create new billing problems.

In March 2026, CMS updated several Medicare TMS billing policies, with revised guidance taking effect around the end of March and beginning of April.

On paper, the change can look like a routine policy update.

For TMS providers, it's worth paying closer attention.

Why?

Because TMS reimbursement isn't just about submitting the correct CPT code. Coverage, documentation, diagnosis requirements, authorization and payer-specific billing rules all play a role in whether that claim actually gets paid.

And that's where things can get messy.

For example:
• CMS's current TMS billing guidance continues to identify 90867, 90868 and 90869 as the core TMS treatment codes.
• Medicare coverage still ties medical necessity to specific diagnoses. CMS's current billing article lists F32.2 and F33.2 among the covered diagnosis codes. Simply attaching a payable procedure code to a claim doesn't guarantee reimbursement.
• Payer requirements can also differ significantly. Highmark, for example, added TMS codes 90867, 90868 and 90869 to its prior authorization requirements effective March 1, 2026, alongside PHP and IOP codes.

That's the trap.

A practice can update its billing rules based on one payer's requirements and still have claims denied by another because the authorization, documentation or medical-necessity rules aren't the same.

And for organizations offering TMS alongside IOP, PHP, Spravato or traditional outpatient psychiatry, the complexity compounds.

Different services.

Different authorization requirements.

Different payer policies.

Different documentation expectations.

Same billing team.

The result can be more rework, more denials, longer payer follow-up and ultimately more money sitting in AR.

TMS providers should be reviewing their payer-specific requirements, not just their CPT codes.

If your billing team updated its TMS workflow this spring but didn't revisit the payer-specific authorization and documentation requirements behind it, that's worth taking another look at.

Sources: CMS Medicare Coverage Database, “Billing and Coding: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation” (current effective date 4/1/2026); Highmark, “Behavioral Health: Upcoming Prior Authorization Changes.”

text_or_description:
A prior authorization was denied.

Okay.

But what happened before that denial?

That’s the part I’m interested in.

When you look at prior authorization data, it’s easy to say: “10 medications were denied this month.” But that number alone doesn’t tell me much.

I want to know why they were denied.

Was it because the medication didn’t meet the insurance company’s criteria?
Was documentation missing?
Was the wrong information submitted?
Did the patient’s medical history support the request?
Were the recent office notes and medication history reviewed before answering the payer’s questions?

Because when you’re working on a prior authorization, you’re not just filling out a form and hoping for an approval.

You’re working with the patient’s clinical information, provider documentation, medication history, and the payer’s requirements.

And sometimes, one missing piece of information can change the outcome.

That’s why I don’t think “approved” or “denied” should be the end of the analysis.

The real question is: What is driving the outcome?

Because a denial is a number.

The story behind that number is where the real insight is.

text_or_description:
𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐁𝐈𝐋𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐆 𝐑𝐎𝐎𝐌
Chapter 4: Prior Authorization 
Part 1 - "Why It Exists and Why Everyone Hates It" 
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━  

A new chapter starts today.  

If credentialing is the gate you have to pass before you can bill, prior authorization is the gate that stands between your patient and their treatment, every single time certain services are ordered.  Nobody in healthcare likes it. Almost everyone deals with it constantly. Very few people actually understand why it exists or how to work with it efficiently.  

𝐖𝐇𝐀𝐓 𝐈𝐒 𝐏𝐑𝐈𝐎𝐑 𝐀𝐔𝐓𝐇𝐎𝐑𝐈𝐙𝐀𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍?  Prior authorization, often called prior auth or PA, is a requirement from the insurance payer that certain services, procedures, or medications must be approved before they are performed or prescribed.  Without that approval, the payer can deny the claim entirely, even if the service was medically necessary and correctly documented.  

𝐖𝐇𝐘 𝐃𝐎𝐄𝐒 𝐈𝐓 𝐄𝐗𝐈𝐒𝐓?  Payers use prior auth as a cost and utilization control mechanism. From their perspective, it prevents unnecessary or inappropriate care, controls high cost procedures and medications, and ensures the requested treatment matches their specific coverage criteria before money is spent.  From the provider and patient perspective, it often feels like a delay tactic that puts a non-clinical reviewer between the doctor and the treatment plan.  Both things are true at the same time. That tension is exactly why prior auth is one of the most frustrating parts of modern healthcare.  

𝐖𝐇𝐀𝐓 𝐓𝐘𝐏𝐈𝐂𝐀𝐋𝐋𝐘 𝐑𝐄𝐐𝐔𝐈𝐑𝐄𝐒 𝐈𝐓  Advanced imaging like MRIs, CTs, and PET scans.  Many surgical procedures, particularly elective ones.  Certain specialty medications, especially biologics and high cost drugs.  Durable medical equipment above certain cost thresholds.  Some physical therapy, chiropractic, and behavioral health services beyond an initial visit count.  Out of network referrals.  Requirements vary significantly by payer, by plan, and by state. What requires auth with one payer may not require it with another for the exact same service.

Prior-Authorization Denials

A denial rate tells you there is a problem.
A denial reason tells you where to look.

A denial rate is an important performance measure—but it is not a diagnosis.

To improve the workflow, organizations need to understand what is underneath that number.

Was documentation missing?

Were coverage requirements misunderstood?

Was the wrong code submitted?

Did the request miss a deadline?

Was additional information requested but never routed to the correct person?

Was the service scheduled before authorization was complete?

CMS’s finalized prior-authorization requirements already require impacted payers to provide a specific reason for denied non-drug prior-authorization decisions beginning in 2026.

Beginning primarily January 1, 2027, the required Prior Authorization APIs must also communicate a specific denial reason electronically.

That creates an opportunity for healthcare organizations to stop treating every denial as the same problem.

Group the reasons.

Identify the workflow responsible.

Assign an owner.

Measure whether the corrective action works.

A team cannot improve a category called “denied.”

It can improve missing documentation, incorrect coding, eligibility errors, untimely follow-up, and failed handoffs.

Do not stop at counting denials. Learn from them.

#PriorAuthorization #DenialManagement #RevenueCycle #PatientAccess #HealthcareAnalytics #WorkflowImprovement

The goal is simple: Better processes. Better patient experiences. Better healthcare.

This is a finalized CMS requirement, not a proposal. CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule⁠￼.

title: LinkedIn post by Maham Saeed
text_or_description:
Are pre-authorization delays and medical necessity denials impacting your cardiology revenue cycle? 💔

Cardiology medical billing is inherently high-stakes. Between expensive diagnostic imaging, complex interventional procedures, and continuous remote monitoring, simple eligibility errors can result in devastating revenue losses.

Verifying basic patient eligibility is no longer enough. To protect your practice from costly write-offs and retrospective audit clawbacks, your front-end team must execute a strict, specialized verification protocol.

Here are the main points to verify for every cardiology patient before care is rendered:

🔹 Payer-Specific Medical Necessity & ICD-10 Alignment – Many major insurers limit coverage for procedures like echocardiograms or myocardial imaging to highly specific clinical indications. Always cross-reference the patient's documented diagnosis code against the payer’s active coverage criteria.

🔹 Prior Authorization for Imaging and Intervention – An estimated 85% of advanced cardiology procedures—including heart catheterizations, cardiac MRIs, and CT scans—require formal prior authorization. Confirm authorization numbers are active in your EHR at least 7 to 14 days before the scheduled procedure date.

🔹 Indication-Specific Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM) Rules – If enrolling a patient in cardiac telemetry or digital health monitoring, check the policy rules at the individual plan level. Some commercial payers strictly limit RPM reimbursement to specific chronic diagnoses like heart failure, while excluding others.

🔹 Referral Mandates for Specialists – Determine if the patient’s plan requires a formal primary care provider (PCP) referral to see a cardiologist. Missing a required electronic referral will trigger an automatic claim denial, even if the policy is active.

🔹 Granular Out-of-Pocket Breakdown – Cardiology treatments carry high patient responsibility. Verify the exact remaining deductible, co-insurance percentages for outpatient hospital settings versus in-office clinics, and the total out-of-pocket maximum.

🔹 Coordination of Benefits (COB) – Always ask if the patient has secondary or tertiary coverage (e.g., commercial plan paired with Medicare). Submitting to the wrong primary payer causes automatic rejection and massive delays.

Shifting from a generalized verification workflow to a specialized cardiology checklist dramatically drops clean-claim denial rates. Clean claims start long before the doctor ever sees the patient!

How has your practice optimized its prior authorization workflow for complex cardiac cases? Let’s share strategies in the comments! 👇

title: LinkedIn post by Ana Lidia Aguilera Hechavarria
text_or_description:
An authorization number is not a paid claim.

Independent radiation oncology, medical oncology, urology, and behavioral health practices still lose cash when the PA, the chart, and the claim tell three different stories. Payers approve a range of codes, units, dates, and providers. Billing often ships something adjacent. That is how you get CO-15 and “auth on file” denials that feel unfair and are usually preventable.

A practical denial-prevention checklist before the claim drops:

Eligibility and PA rules checked for this plan and this service, in the right portal, not last month’s screenshot.
The approved PA record matches what you will bill: CPT/HCPCS, units, diagnosis, rendering and facility NPI, place of service, and date span. If the plan approved 77412 and the claim says 77407, you already lost.
Clinical documentation supports the request the payer approved. Radiation: technique, dose, fractionation, and image guidance line up with the prescription. Oncology drugs and imaging: staging, intent, and biomarkers sit in the chart the way the policy asks, not as a vague “positive” note. Behavioral health: level of care, functional impairment, and why a lower level failed or is contraindicated, plus concurrent review dates if the auth is episode-based.
Do not schedule infusion, radiation starts, or high-cost imaging without a live PA when the payer requires one. Expired or unit-exhausted auths should stop the charge, not surprise the remittance.
Before batch, reconcile auth to claim. After denials, bucket CO-15 by root cause (no PA, provider mismatch, dx mismatch, units exceeded, expired) and fix the gate that owns it.

Getting the letter is step one. Getting paid is matching the letter to the claim.

title: LinkedIn post by Girish G. Kaimal Pharm D., MBA, FACHE, FHFMA
text_or_description:
#UnitedHealthcare is removing prior authorization requirements for roughly 1,700 procedure codes effective October 1, 2026. 

That is welcome news. But what happened to the patients who needed that care before the requirements were removed?

The company told Healthcare Dive it focused on services with established clinical efficacy and consistently high approval rates. 

An approval rate tells us how often permission was granted. It does not tell us what waiting for permission cost the patient.

UnitedHealthcare’s own explanation includes removing “barriers that can delay care.” 

That deserves more than an administrative-burden discussion.

For these specific services, how many patients experienced avoidable delays? How many abandoned treatment? Was preventable harm tracked, and did those findings inform the decision to remove the requirements?

The announcement does not provide that accounting. 

In the #AMA’s 2025 survey of 1,000 physicians, 26% reported that prior authorization had led to a serious adverse event for a patient in their care. These are physician reports across payers, not a harm estimate for UnitedHealthcare or these codes. 

They are a reason to ask for more than a count of requirements eliminated.

#CMS already requires aggregate reporting of approvals, appeals and decision times from #Medicare Advantage, Medicaid/CHIP and federally facilitated exchange payers, excluding drug authorizations. UnitedHealthcare says it has published those metrics. 

Now break them out for the codes being removed. For employer plans outside that federal reporting requirement, publish the same breakdown.

And measure more than the insurer’s decision clock.

CMS measures that clock from receipt of a request to a determination. That is not the same as time from a treatment decision to treatment. 

An approval after an appeal may correct a coverage decision. It cannot give a patient back the days spent waiting.

Preventing unnecessary or unsafe care matters. For the requirements that remain, what evidence shows the review improves care enough to justify its burden? What findings trigger an independent review, suspension or removal?

Health systems and employers purchasing coverage should be asking these questions, too.

When a patient abandons necessary treatment, we should not mistake the absence of a claim for successful care management.

The burden of proof should not rest only with the clinician requesting care.

It should also rest with the organization requiring permission.

title: LinkedIn post by Chris Cockey
text_or_description:
Medicare Advantage plan operations are becoming easier for the public to see.
Prior authorization is the process through which a plan reviews certain services before agreeing to cover them. It has long been difficult for beneficiaries and advisors to evaluate how that process operates across Medicare Advantage contracts.
A KFF analysis published in January 2026 examined CMS contract-level data for 2024. Medicare Advantage insurers made 52.8 million prior authorization decisions:
- 92.3% of requests were approved in full
- 7.7% were not fully approved
- 11.5% of denials were appealed
- When someone asked the plan to look again, it changed its original answer 80.7% of the time
In public-facing terms, when someone asked the plan to look again, the plan approved all or part of the requested care in more than 8 out of 10 appeals.
The figure needs context. A changed decision does not automatically establish that the first decision was improper; an appeal may include additional clinical documentation. The data are also aggregated at the Medicare Advantage contract level and cannot predict the result of an individual request.
But the scale and appeal results demonstrate why transparency matters.
Beginning in 2026, Medicare Advantage organizations must publicly report approval and denial rates, appeal outcomes, and response times for medical items and services, excluding drugs. CMS has also said that this information must be publicly accessible and understandable to patients.
This is a positive development in Medicare oversight. Public reporting will not resolve every problem with prior authorization, but it creates a stronger basis for accountability and better-informed plan reviews.
